newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Sweden can't ban TV child ads from abroad-EU court.
newsitem.headline: Sweden can't ban TV child ads from abroad-EU court.

text.p: The European Court of Justice ruled on Wednesday that Sweden, which bans TV advertising aimed at children, cannot block such commercials broadcast from another European Union member state.
Swedish Consumer Ombudsman Axel Edling described the verdict as a "setback" to the country's ban on advertising directed towards children under the age of twelve.
"I'm disappointed that Sweden will not be able to maintain consumer protection for children," he told the Swedish news agency TT in Stockholm.

But Swedish Culture Minister Marita Ulvskog vowed to continue to try and convince other EU countries about the need for such a ban. "This is an enormously important issue for Sweden and we will not give up," she said in Stockholm.

Sweden has argued that children cannot always differ between advertisements and TV programmes. It is the only EU country that has a general ban on advertising aimed at children while Greece bans advertising for toys.

The Luxembourg-based EU court said an EU member state "may penalise an advertiser on account of misleading advertising coming from another member state but may not do so simply on the ground that the advertising is directed at children."
But there was nothing in the EU's Television without Frontiers law to prevent Stockholm from applying stricter rules for broadcasters based in Sweden.

"The decision of the court confirms that Sweden may not take measures to ban advertising to children broadcast from other member states but, anomalously, that it may do so only for broadcasters within its own border," said Peter Waterman, chairman of the broadcasting committee at the Toy Industries of Europe, a trade association.

The court had been asked to decide whether EU law allowed Sweden to bar advertisements aired by a TV channel based in a member state where they are legal and also whether the Swedish ban constituted a trade barrier and was therefore contrary to the EU's Treaty of Rome.

The case involved an advertisement for a magazine about dinosaurs that publishing firm De Agostini Forlag AB aired on television channels TV3 and TV4 in 1993. TV3 is a British-based channel broadcasting to Sweden while TV4 is based in Sweden.
Edling, saying the advertisement should be banned, decided to take De Agostini to the Swedish Market Court, which asked for a preliminary ruling from the EU court.
Lawyer Peter Danowsky, who represented De Agostini, said the EU court's ruling meant that Sweden could not intervene against commercials aimed at children broadcast on TV3.
But he added that the Swedish ban on advertising aimed at children in principle continued to be in force for TV4.
"That of course affects the competitive situation between TV3 and TV4," he said in a statement.
Europe's advertising industry saw the case as a critical test of its right to provide services across the EU.
The court battle is a sign of the realities of the new television age with authorities unable to control the contents of programmes broadcast from another country.
